questions.stem: Two point charges exert a force F on each other. One charge is tripled and the separation is halved. The new force is:
questions.explanation: Tripling one charge multiplies F by 3, and halving r multiplies it by 4 (inverse square), so F becomes 12F. 6F misses the square on r, 3F/4 puts the factor on the wrong side, and 3F/2 mixes the two errors.

questions.stem: A battery with an open-circuit voltage of 9.0 V delivers 2.0 A with a terminal voltage of 6.0 V. What is its internal resistance?
questions.explanation: The lost voltage is 9.0 - 6.0 = 3.0 V across r, so r = 3.0 V/2.0 A = 1.5 ohm. 3.0 ohm is the external resistance (6.0/2.0), 4.5 ohm would be 9.0/2.0 (the total resistance), and 0.67 ohm inverts the ratio.

questions.stem: A 2.0 uF capacitor discharges through a 1.0 megohm resistor. About how long does it take for the voltage to fall to half its starting value?
questions.explanation: tau = RC = 2.0 s and the half-time is tau ln 2 = 0.693 x 2.0 = 1.4 s. 2.0 s is the time to reach 37 percent, 0.50 s inverts tau, and 4.0 s is 2 tau (13.5 percent left).

questions.stem: A 0.20 m wire carrying 4.0 A is perpendicular to a 0.30 T field. The magnetic force on the wire is:
questions.explanation: F = BIL sin 90 = (0.30)(4.0)(0.20) = 0.24 N. 0.060 N is B x L x 1 (forgetting the current), 0.015 N is a misplaced decimal, and 3.8 N inverts the arithmetic.
questions.subtopic: Magnetic force on charges and currents (right-hand rule)

questions.stem: Three metals have standard reduction potentials A+/A = +0.50 V, B2+/B = -0.20 V, and C+/C = -1.00 V. Which pair gives a galvanic cell with the largest E0 cell?
questions.explanation: The largest E0 comes from the most negative anode and the most positive cathode: 0.50 - (-1.00) = 1.50 V with C as the anode and A as the cathode. The 0.70 V and 0.80 V pairs are galvanic but smaller, and the last pair reverses the roles, giving a negative (nonspontaneous) value.
questions.subtopic: Standard reduction potentials and cell EMF

demo_cards.front: Magnitude of the electrostatic force between two point charges?
demo_cards.back: F = k q<sub>1</sub>q<sub>2</sub>/r<sup>2</sup>, with k = 9.0 x 10<sup>9</sup> N m<sup>2</sup>/C<sup>2</sup>.

demo_cards.text: Coulomb's law: F = {{c1::k q<sub>1</sub>q<sub>2</sub>/r<sup>2</sup>}}, where k = {{c2::9.0 x 10<sup>9</sup> N m<sup>2</sup>/C<sup>2</sup>}}.
demo_cards.extra: In terms of permittivity, k = 1/(4 pi e0).

demo_cards.stem: A +2.0 uC charge and a -3.0 uC charge are 0.30 m apart. The force between them is:
demo_cards.why: F = (9.0 x 10<sup>9</sup>)(2.0 x 10<sup>-6</sup>)(3.0 x 10<sup>-6</sup>)/(0.30)<sup>2</sup> = 0.60 N. Opposite signs attract. Trap: using centimeters or dropping the micro prefix.

demo_cards.statement: Net charge in an isolated system stays constant, even when charge moves between objects.
demo_cards.why: Charge is conserved. It can be transferred but not created or destroyed.
